units.title: Letters, vowels and silent letters
goals: Explain why French spelling can be read aloud by rules even though it cannot always be written from sound
Say the name of every letter and spell a name aloud
Say the oral vowels and read each of their spellings, including 'ou', 'eu', 'au', 'eau' and 'ai', and read 'oi' as [wa]
Tell which final letters are silent: a final 'e', most final consonants, and the letters 'c', 'r', 'f' and 'l' that are usually pronounced
grammar: The alphabet: 26 letters and their French names, and how marks, double letters and the apostrophe are named when spelling aloud
Spelling as a code: why reading French from the page is regular and writing it from sound is not
The oral vowels [a] [i] [e] [ɛ] [o] [ɔ] [u] [y] [ø] [œ] [ə] and their spellings ('é', 'è', 'ê', 'ai', 'ei', 'au', 'eau', 'ou', 'u', 'eu', 'œu'), and 'oi' [wa] and 'ui' [ɥi]
The two vowels English lacks, [y] and [ø], and the pair 'u' and 'ou' ('la rue', 'la roue')
Silent letters: final 'e', final consonants, the plural 's', and the usually pronounced final 'c', 'r', 'f' and 'l'
vocabulary_themes: words chosen only to illustrate each vowel and each silent letter
letter names and spelling a name aloud
pairs of words that differ by one vowel

units.title: Nasal vowels and consonants
goals: Say the three nasal vowels and recognize every spelling of each
Tell when 'n' or 'm' makes the vowel before it nasal and when it is an ordinary consonant ('bon', 'bonne')
Apply the rules for the consonants whose sound depends on the next letter: 'c', 'ç', 'g', 'ge', 'gu', 'qu', 's', 'ss' and 'x'
Read the letter groups 'ch', 'gn', 'ill', 'ph', 'th' and the French 'r'
Read aloud an unfamiliar word by following a fixed procedure
grammar: Nasal vowels [ɑ̃] [ɔ̃] [ɛ̃] and their spellings ('an', 'am', 'en', 'em', 'on', 'om', 'in', 'im', 'ain', 'ein', 'un', 'um'), and the older fourth vowel [œ̃]
Denasalization: a vowel plus 'n' or 'm' is oral when a vowel or a second 'n' or 'm' follows ('bon' and 'bonne', 'plein' and 'pleine')
Consonants chosen by the next letter: 'c' and 'ç', 'g', 'ge' and 'gu', 'qu', single 's' between vowels versus 'ss', and 'x'
Letter groups and semivowels: 'ch', 'gn', 'ill', 'ph', 'th', '-tion', the glides in 'oui', 'payer' and 'le chien', and the uvular 'r'
A procedure for reading any new word
vocabulary_themes: words chosen only to illustrate each nasal vowel and each consonant rule
pairs of words that differ by one sound ('le poisson', 'le poison')

units.title: Accent marks, rhythm, liaison and elision
goals: Explain what each mark does: acute, grave, circumflex, diaeresis and cedilla
Explain why French marks never show stress, and where the stress of a group of words falls
Explain why words such as 'l’hôpital', 'la forêt', 'où', 'à', 'là', 'sûr', 'Noël' and 'naïf' are written as they are
Apply elision and the common cases of liaison, and recognize a mute 'h' and an aspirated 'h'
grammar: The acute accent on 'é', the grave accent on 'è', 'à' and 'ù', the circumflex on any vowel, the diaeresis on 'ë', 'ï' and 'ü', and the cedilla on 'ç'
The circumflex as the trace of a lost 's' ('la forêt' and English 'forest', 'l’hôpital' and English 'hospital')
Marks that only tell words apart: 'a' and 'à', 'ou' and 'où', 'la' and 'là', 'sur' and 'sûr', 'du' and 'dû'
Rhythm: syllables of equal length, no word stress, and a stronger final syllable in each group of words
Linking: elision ('l’', 'j’', 'd’', 'n’', 'qu’'), the carrying of a final consonant into the next word ('l’enchaînement'), required and forbidden liaison, mute and aspirated 'h'
The 1990 spelling reform and the traditional spelling this course uses
vocabulary_themes: words whose mark distinguishes them from another word
words that begin with a vowel or an 'h' and show elision and liaison

units.title: How French works: the big picture
goals: Know the vocabulary of grammar used throughout this course: noun, article, adjective, verb, infinitive, conjugation, person, number, tense, mood, pronoun, preposition, clause, agreement, contraction
See how a French sentence is built and where it differs from English
Understand gender, number and agreement, and why the article carries the number in speech
Understand that verbs change for person and tense and that the subject pronoun is never dropped
Make a sentence negative with 'ne' and 'pas' and a yes-or-no question with rising intonation
grammar: Parts of speech and the terms of grammar used in the course
Word order: subject, verb, object; most adjectives after the noun; object pronouns before the verb (a first look)
Gender and number: every noun is masculine or feminine; articles and adjectives agree; a written plural is often silent
Verbs: the infinitive ('-er', '-ir', '-re'), conjugation by person and number, and the required subject pronoun
Negation with 'ne' before the verb and 'pas' after it; questions by intonation
Contractions of 'à' and 'de' with the articles 'le' and 'les' ('au', 'aux', 'du', 'des')
vocabulary_themes: the words for the parts of speech, in English and French
the very small set of function words used in every sentence ('le', 'la', 'les', 'un', 'une', 'de', 'et', 'ne', 'pas')

units.title: Greetings and introductions
goals: Greet people and say goodbye, formally and informally
Introduce yourself, ask someone's name and say that you are pleased to meet them
Say where you are from and what nationality you are
Choose between 'tu' and 'vous', and use the present tense of 'être'
Use the basic politeness expressions and know what each literally says
grammar: Subject pronouns ('je', 'tu', 'il', 'elle', 'on', 'nous', 'vous', 'ils', 'elles') and what 'on' means
'Tu' versus 'vous': one person or several, familiar or formal
Present tense of 'être' ('je suis', 'tu es', 'il est', 'nous sommes', 'vous êtes', 'ils sont')
Nationality adjectives and their feminine forms ('français' and 'française'), written with a lowercase letter
Fixed phrases used before their grammar: 'je m’appelle', 'comment tu t’appelles', 'j’habite à', 'et toi', 'et vous', 'voici'

units.title: Être, avoir and how you feel
goals: Say how you feel and describe people with adjectives
Use 'avoir' where English uses 'be' for hunger, thirst, heat, cold, fear and being right
Make adjectives agree with the noun or pronoun they describe
Make sentences negative, and know how the word 'ne' is dropped in everyday speech
Ask simple questions with 'qui', 'comment' and 'où'
grammar: Present tense of 'avoir' ('j’ai', 'tu as', 'il a', 'nous avons', 'vous avez', 'ils ont') and the liaison that separates 'ils ont' from 'ils sont'
'Avoir' plus a noun for physical states and feelings ('avoir faim', 'avoir peur', 'avoir raison')
Adjective agreement: '-e' and '-s', adjectives already ending in '-e', '-eux' and '-euse', 'gentil' and 'gentille', and the final consonant that becomes audible in the feminine
Negation 'ne... pas' with elision ('je n’ai pas'), and the spoken form without 'ne'
'C’est' plus an adjective versus 'il est' and 'elle est' plus an adjective

units.title: Numbers, time and dates
goals: Count from 0 to 100, including the numbers built on twenty
Say your age and a telephone number
Tell the time in the everyday and the 24-hour systems
Say days, months and dates
grammar: Cardinal numbers 0 to 100: 'soixante-dix', 'quatre-vingts', 'quatre-vingt-dix', 'vingt et un', the hyphens, and the final consonants of 'cinq', 'six', 'huit' and 'dix'
Age with 'avoir': 'j’ai vingt ans', with 'quel âge as-tu' as a fixed phrase until inversion is taught
Telling time: 'il est deux heures', 'et quart', 'et demie', 'moins le quart', 'midi', 'minuit', and the 24-hour clock, with 'quelle heure est-il' as a fixed phrase
Days of the week and months without capitals; dates with 'le' and a cardinal number, except 'le premier'
The interrogative 'quel' in 'quelle heure' and 'quel âge'
vocabulary_themes: days of the week and months
parts of the day ('le matin', 'l’après-midi', 'le soir')

units.title: Verbs in '-er': work, study and languages
goals: Conjugate the regular '-er' verbs in the present and know which forms sound alike
Say what you do, where you work or study and which languages you speak
Ask questions in three ways: by intonation, with 'est-ce que' and by inversion
Say what you like and dislike with 'aimer', 'adorer' and 'détester'
grammar: Regular '-er' verbs in the present ('parle', 'parles', 'parle', 'parlons', 'parlez', 'parlent'), with four forms said alike
Elision and liaison with verbs that begin with a vowel ('j’habite', 'nous aimons')
Questions by intonation, with 'est-ce que', and by inversion with the linking 't' ('parle-t-il')
Question words 'quand' and 'pourquoi' beside 'qui', 'comment' and 'où', and the question phrase 'qu’est-ce que'
'Aimer' plus the definite article for things in general, and 'aimer' plus an infinitive
Professions after 'être' without an article ('il est médecin') versus 'c’est un médecin'

units.title: Family, articles and possessives
goals: Talk about your family
Use the definite and indefinite articles and form plurals
Say whose something is with possessive words, with 'de' and with 'à moi'
Use the stressed pronouns after prepositions and in short answers
grammar: Definite articles ('le', 'la', 'l’', 'les') and indefinite articles ('un', 'une', 'des')
Plurals: a silent '-s', '-eau' to '-eaux', '-al' to '-aux', and nouns that do not change

Possessive determiners ('mon', 'ma', 'mes', 'ton', 'ta', 'tes', 'son', 'sa', 'ses', 'notre', 'nos', 'votre', 'vos', 'leur', 'leurs'), agreeing with the thing possessed, and 'mon' before a feminine noun that begins with a vowel
Possession with 'de' ('la voiture de Léa', 'le frère du professeur')
Stressed pronouns ('moi', 'toi', 'lui', 'elle', 'nous', 'vous', 'eux', 'elles') after prepositions, after 'c’est', with 'aussi', and in 'à moi'

units.title: Food, drinks and ordering
goals: Order in a café, a bakery and a restaurant
Say what you want, what you take and what you drink
Talk about an amount of something with the partitive article and with words of quantity
Ask for the bill
grammar: The partitive article ('du', 'de la', 'de l’', 'des') for an amount of something, and the definite article for a thing in general
'De' after a negation ('pas de café') and after words of quantity ('beaucoup de', 'un peu de', 'un verre de', 'un kilo de')
Present tense of 'prendre', 'boire' and 'vouloir'
Polite ordering with 'je voudrais' (a fixed phrase until the conditional) and 'pour moi'

units.title: Daily routine
goals: Describe a typical day
Use pronominal verbs such as 'se lever' and 'se coucher'
Say how often you do something
Ask about someone's routine and schedule
grammar: Pronominal verbs in the present ('je me lève', 'tu te lèves', 'il se lève', 'nous nous levons', 'vous vous levez', 'ils se lèvent') and their negative
Spelling changes in '-er' verbs: 'lever' and 'acheter' with 'è', 'préférer' with 'è', 'appeler' with 'll', 'manger' with 'ge' and 'commencer' with 'ç' before 'a' and 'o'
Present tense of 'faire' and its uses ('faire la cuisine', 'faire les courses')
Frequency adverbs after the verb ('toujours', 'souvent', 'parfois') and the negation 'ne... jamais'
Time expressions: 'à sept heures', 'vers midi', 'le lundi', 'du lundi au vendredi', 'tous les jours'

units.title: Places and directions
goals: Name places in a town
Ask for and give directions
Say where things are
Use 'aller' and 'venir' with the contractions of 'à' and 'de'
grammar: Present tense of 'aller' and 'venir'
'À' and 'de' after 'aller' and 'venir': the contractions 'au', 'aux', 'du' and 'des' beside 'à la', 'à l’', 'de la' and 'de l’'
'Il y a' for what exists in a place, and 'il n’y a pas de'
Prepositions of place: 'dans', 'devant', 'derrière', 'entre', 'près de', 'loin de', 'à côté de', 'en face de', 'au coin de'
The imperative for directions: 'tournez', 'prenez', 'allez', 'continuez', and the forms for 'tu': 'tourne', 'prends', 'va'
Ordinal numbers ('premier', 'deuxième', 'troisième')

units.title: Shopping, clothes and colors
goals: Ask for prices and sizes
Describe clothes and their colors
Point things out with demonstratives and ask which one with 'quel'
Use the regular '-ir' and '-re' verbs
grammar: Demonstratives 'ce', 'cet', 'cette', 'ces', and '-ci' and '-là' for near and far
The interrogative 'quel', 'quelle', 'quels', 'quelles'
Colors after the noun with agreement, and the invariable 'marron' and 'orange'
Regular '-ir' verbs like 'choisir' ('nous choisissons') and '-re' verbs like 'vendre' ('il vend')
Numbers from 100 to a million, prices in euros, and 'combien'
Verbs in '-yer': 'payer' and 'essayer' ('je paie', 'j’essaie')

units.title: Home and housing
goals: Describe your home and its rooms
Say where furniture and objects are
Rent or ask about an apartment
Place adjectives before or after the noun correctly
grammar: Adjectives before the noun ('beau', 'joli', 'bon', 'mauvais', 'grand', 'petit', 'jeune', 'vieux', 'nouveau') and after it
The forms 'bel', 'nouvel' and 'vieil' before a vowel, and the feminines 'belle', 'nouvelle' and 'vieille'
Prepositions 'sur', 'sous', 'dans' and 'chez' ('chez moi', 'chez Léa')
'Avoir besoin de' and 'il y a' in descriptions
Floors: 'le rez-de-chaussée', 'au premier étage'
vocabulary_themes: rooms and parts of a home

units.title: Plans, weather and leisure
goals: Talk about plans with 'aller' plus an infinitive
Say what you can, must and know how to do
Talk about the weather
Invite someone, accept and decline politely
grammar: The near future: 'aller' plus an infinitive ('je vais partir', 'je ne vais pas sortir', 'je vais me coucher')
Present tense of 'pouvoir', 'devoir' and 'savoir', each with an infinitive
'Savoir' versus 'connaître'
Verbs like 'partir', 'sortir' and 'dormir' ('je pars', 'nous partons')
Weather with the impersonal 'il': 'il fait beau', 'il pleut', 'il neige', 'il fait vingt degrés'
Invitations: 'on va au cinéma', 'tu veux venir', 'ça te dit', 'volontiers', 'désolé, je ne peux pas'

units.title: A1 consolidation
goals: Combine everything from A1 in longer conversations
Connect sentences with 'et', 'mais', 'donc', 'alors', 'parce que' and 'si'
Avoid the most common beginner errors
Talk about yourself, your family, your day and your plans in a short connected text
grammar: Review: pronouns, 'être', 'avoir', 'aller', 'faire', the regular present, articles, contractions and the near future
Review of the three ways to ask a question
Common beginner errors: 'avoir' where English has 'be', missing articles, agreement, 'c’est' versus 'il est'
Connecting sentences with 'et', 'mais', 'donc', 'alors', 'parce que' and 'si' plus the present

units.title: The compound past with 'avoir'
goals: Say what you did with the compound past
Form the past participle of regular verbs and learn the common irregular ones
Place the negation and short adverbs in a compound tense
Tell a short sequence of events
grammar: The compound past ('le passé composé'): the present of 'avoir' plus the past participle, for English 'I did' and 'I have done'
Regular participles ('parlé', 'fini', 'vendu') and irregular ones ('eu', 'été', 'fait', 'pris', 'mis', 'vu', 'lu', 'bu', 'dit', 'écrit', 'pu', 'voulu', 'dû', 'su', 'connu')
Negation and adverbs around the auxiliary ('je n’ai pas mangé', 'j’ai déjà mangé')
Past time markers: 'hier', 'la semaine dernière', 'il y a deux jours'
Sequencing with 'd’abord', 'ensuite', 'puis' and 'enfin'

units.title: The compound past with 'être'
goals: Know which verbs form the compound past with 'être'
Make the participle agree with the subject
Use pronominal verbs in the past
Tell the story of a journey or of a life
grammar: The verbs of movement and change of state with 'être' ('aller', 'venir', 'arriver', 'partir', 'entrer', 'sortir', 'monter', 'descendre', 'naître', 'mourir', 'rester', 'tomber', 'retourner', 'rentrer', 'revenir', 'devenir')
Agreement of the participle with the subject ('elle est partie', 'ils sont arrivés'), and agreement with 'on'
Pronominal verbs with 'être' ('je me suis levé', 'elle s’est réveillée')
'Monter', 'descendre', 'sortir' and 'rentrer' with 'avoir' when they have a direct object

units.title: Nothing, nobody, never: negation and indefinite words
goals: Use the negations 'ne... rien', 'ne... personne', 'ne... plus', 'ne... pas encore', 'ne... aucun' and 'ne... nulle part', and say 'only' with 'ne... que'
Place each negation correctly in simple and compound tenses
Use 'quelque chose', 'quelqu’un', 'quelque part' and 'tout'
Answer 'si' to a negative question
grammar: Two-part negations and their placement ('je n’ai rien vu', 'je n’ai vu personne')
Negative words as subjects and alone ('Personne n’est venu', 'Rien ne marche', 'Jamais.')
'Ne... que' meaning 'only', which is not a negation
Indefinite words: 'quelque chose de bon', 'quelqu’un de gentil', 'tout', 'toute', 'tous', 'toutes', 'tout le monde'
'Si' to contradict a negative question, the question phrase 'qu’est-ce qui', and the dropped 'ne' with these words in speech

units.title: The imperfect: habits and descriptions
goals: Form the imperfect from the present form for 'nous'
Describe how things were and what you used to do
Talk about your childhood
Contrast then and now with 'ne... plus'
grammar: The imperfect: the stem of the present form for 'nous' plus '-ais', '-ais', '-ait', '-ions', '-iez', '-aient', with four forms said alike; 'être' with the stem 'ét-'
Spelling in the imperfect: 'je mangeais', 'je commençais'
Uses: habits, descriptions, states, age, time and weather in the past
Then and now: 'quand j’étais petit', 'avant', 'maintenant', 'ne... plus'

units.title: Compound past versus imperfect
goals: Choose between the compound past and the imperfect in a story
Describe an action in progress with 'être en train de'
Say that something has just happened with 'venir de'
Tell a short story with a setting, an event and a result
grammar: Event versus background: 'je lisais quand le téléphone a sonné'
'Être en train de' plus an infinitive, in the present and the imperfect
'Venir de' plus an infinitive for the recent past ('je viens de manger', 'je venais de partir')
Verbs whose meaning shifts in the compound past: 'savoir', 'connaître', 'pouvoir', 'vouloir'
Story connectors: 'soudain', 'tout à coup', 'pendant que', 'ce jour-là'

units.title: Direct and indirect object pronouns
goals: Replace a direct object with 'le', 'la', 'l’' or 'les', and an indirect object with 'lui' or 'leur'
Place object pronouns before the verb, before an infinitive and before the auxiliary
Know which verbs take 'à' before a person, unlike their English equivalents
Make the past participle agree with a direct object placed before it
grammar: Direct object pronouns 'me', 'te', 'le', 'la', 'l’', 'nous', 'vous', 'les'
Indirect object pronouns 'me', 'te', 'lui', 'nous', 'vous', 'leur'
Placement: 'je le vois', 'je ne le vois pas', 'je vais le voir', 'je l’ai vu'
Verbs with 'à' before a person ('téléphoner à', 'répondre à', 'demander à', 'dire à') and verbs with a direct object where English differs ('aider', 'attendre', 'écouter', 'regarder', 'chercher')
Agreement with a preceding direct object ('je les ai vues'), audible only in some participles ('mise', 'prise', 'faite', 'écrite')

units.title: Travel and the pronouns 'y' and 'en'
goals: Use the right preposition with a city or a country
Name means of transport with 'en' and 'à'
Replace a place or a phrase with 'à' by 'y', and a phrase with 'de' or a quantity by 'en'
Book a ticket and a room, and ask about a journey
grammar: Prepositions with places: 'à Paris', 'en France', 'au Canada', 'aux États-Unis', and 'de', 'du', 'des' for origin
Transport: 'en train', 'en voiture', 'en avion', 'à pied', 'à vélo'
The pronoun 'y' ('j’y vais', 'on y va', 'j’y pense')
The pronoun 'en' ('j’en veux', 'j’en ai deux', 'il y en a', 'j’en viens')
Placement of 'y' and 'en' in simple and compound tenses

units.title: Health, the body and the imperative
goals: Name the parts of the body and say where it hurts
Describe symptoms to a doctor or a pharmacist
Give and understand advice and instructions with the imperative
Place pronouns correctly with an affirmative and a negative imperative
grammar: 'Avoir mal à' plus the body part ('j’ai mal à la tête', 'au dos', 'aux dents')
The definite article with parts of the body ('je me lave les mains', 'il s’est cassé la jambe')
'Il faut' plus an infinitive, an impersonal verb with only the subject 'il'
The imperative of all verbs, the form for 'tu' of '-er' verbs without '-s', and the irregular 'sois', 'aie', 'sache'
Pronouns after an affirmative imperative ('prends-le', 'dis-lui', 'couche-toi', 'vas-y') and before a negative one ('ne le prends pas')
vocabulary_themes: at the doctor's and the pharmacy

units.title: Comparing things and people
goals: Compare qualities, quantities and actions
Use 'meilleur' and 'mieux' correctly
Say which is the best or the most of a group
Form adverbs in '-ment' and use the possessive pronouns
grammar: 'Plus', 'moins' and 'aussi' plus an adjective or an adverb plus 'que'; 'plus de', 'moins de' and 'autant de' plus a noun; 'plus que', 'moins que' and 'autant que' after a verb
Irregular comparisons: 'bon' and 'meilleur', 'bien' and 'mieux', 'mauvais' and 'pire'
Superlatives with 'le plus' and 'le moins', their position and 'de' after them ('la plus belle ville du pays')
Adverbs in '-ment' built on the feminine adjective, and '-amment' and '-emment'
Possessive pronouns ('le mien', 'la mienne', 'le tien', 'le sien', 'le nôtre', 'le vôtre', 'le leur')

units.title: Work: 'depuis' and the relative pronouns 'qui', 'que' and 'où'
goals: Say how long something has been going on with 'depuis' and the present
Talk about jobs, companies and working life
Join two sentences with 'qui', 'que' and 'où'
Use the verbs that need 'à' or 'de' before an infinitive
grammar: 'Depuis' plus the present where English uses 'have been doing'; 'ça fait... que', 'il y a... que'; 'pendant' and 'pour'
Relative pronouns 'qui' (subject), 'que' (object) and 'où' (place and time)

Verbs with 'à' plus an infinitive ('apprendre à', 'réussir à', 'commencer à') and with 'de' ('arrêter de', 'accepter de', 'refuser de', 'essayer de', 'oublier de'), and verbs with none ('aimer', 'vouloir', 'pouvoir')

units.title: The future
goals: Form the simple future of regular and irregular verbs
Talk about plans, predictions and promises
Use the future after 'quand' where English uses the present
Make a real condition with 'si' plus the present and the future
grammar: The simple future: the infinitive plus '-ai', '-as', '-a', '-ons', '-ez', '-ont', and '-re' verbs without their final 'e'
Irregular stems: 'ser-', 'aur-', 'ir-', 'fer-', 'viendr-', 'verr-', 'pourr-', 'voudr-', 'devr-', 'saur-', 'enverr-', 'faudr-'
The simple future versus 'aller' plus an infinitive
'Quand', 'lorsque' and 'dès que' plus the future
'Si' plus the present, then the future, and never the future after 'si' meaning 'if'

units.title: The conditional: polite requests and hypotheses
goals: Form the conditional from the future stem and the imperfect endings
Make polite requests and wishes
Give advice with 'tu devrais' and 'à ta place'
Imagine a situation with 'si' plus the imperfect and the conditional
grammar: The present conditional: the future stem plus '-ais', '-ais', '-ait', '-ions', '-iez', '-aient'
Politeness: 'je voudrais', 'j’aimerais', 'pourriez-vous', 'auriez-vous'
Advice: 'tu devrais', 'vous pourriez', 'à ta place, je'
Hypotheses: 'si' plus the imperfect, then the conditional ('si j’avais le temps, je voyagerais')
Telling 'je parlerai' from 'je parlerais' by sound and by context

units.title: A2 consolidation
goals: Tell a past event with both past tenses and object pronouns
Talk about the future and about imagined situations
Write short messages and emails with simple structure
Avoid the most common A2 errors
grammar: Review: compound past, imperfect, object pronouns, 'y' and 'en', imperative, comparisons, future and conditional
Connectors: 'pourtant', 'par contre', 'grâce à', 'à cause de', 'quand même', 'd’ailleurs', 'en fait'
Common A2 errors: the auxiliary, 'depuis', 'quand' plus the future, pronoun placement, agreement
Openings and closings of informal messages ('Salut', 'Chère Sophie', 'Bises', 'Amitiés')

units.title: The present subjunctive: necessity and will
goals: Explain what the subjunctive mood is and why French needs it
Form the present subjunctive of regular, two-stem and irregular verbs
Express necessity, wishes, requests and permission
Choose between an infinitive and 'que' plus the subjunctive
grammar: The subjunctive mood: the indicative states a fact; the subjunctive presents an action as wanted, required, feared or doubted
Formation from the stem of the present form for 'ils' ('ils parlent', 'que je parle') with '-e', '-es', '-e', '-ions', '-iez', '-ent'
Two-stem verbs ('que je vienne', 'que nous venions'; 'prenne', 'boive', 'doive')
Irregular verbs: 'être', 'avoir', 'aller', 'faire', 'pouvoir', 'savoir', 'vouloir', 'falloir'
Triggers: 'il faut que', 'vouloir que', 'souhaiter que', 'exiger que', 'il vaut mieux que', 'il est important que', and 'espérer que', which takes the indicative
Same subject: an infinitive ('je veux partir'); different subject: 'que' plus the subjunctive ('je veux que tu partes')

units.title: Subjunctive: emotion, doubt and conjunctions
goals: React to events with emotion followed by the subjunctive
Choose between the indicative and the subjunctive after 'penser', 'croire' and 'douter'
Use the conjunctions that require the subjunctive
Recognize the 'ne' that is not a negation
grammar: Emotion: 'je suis content que', 'c’est dommage que', 'avoir peur que', 'regretter que'
Doubt and certainty: 'je doute que' and 'je ne pense pas que' with the subjunctive; 'je pense que', 'je crois que' and 'je suis sûr que' with the indicative
Conjunctions with the subjunctive: 'pour que', 'avant que', 'jusqu’à ce que', 'bien que', 'à condition que', 'à moins que', 'sans que'; 'après que' with the indicative
Preposition plus infinitive for the same subject ('pour partir', 'avant de partir', 'sans dire'), and the past infinitive after 'après' ('après avoir mangé')
The expletive 'ne' after 'avant que', 'à moins que' and 'avoir peur que'
vocabulary_themes: a wedding and a family celebration

units.title: Combining pronouns
goals: Use two object pronouns together in the right order
Combine pronouns with an affirmative imperative
Use pronoun combinations in compound tenses and with infinitives
Choose between 'amener', 'emmener', 'apporter' and 'emporter'
grammar: Order before the verb: 'me', 'te', 'se', 'nous', 'vous', then 'le', 'la', 'les', then 'lui', 'leur', then 'y', then 'en' ('il me le donne', 'je le lui ai dit', 'il y en a')
Order after an affirmative imperative ('donne-le-moi', 'donnez-m’en', 'vas-y')
Pronoun pairs with compound tenses and infinitives ('je vais te le prêter', 'je te l’ai rendu')
Verbs of carrying and bringing: people versus things, towards versus away
Fixed pronominal expressions: 's’en aller', 'je vous en prie'

units.title: Relative clauses: 'dont', 'lequel' and 'ce qui'
goals: Use 'dont' for a relative clause built on 'de'
Use 'lequel' and its forms after a preposition
Say 'what' inside a sentence with 'ce qui', 'ce que' and 'ce dont'
Point to people and things with 'celui', 'celle', 'ceux' and 'celles'
grammar: 'Dont' ('le livre dont je parle', 'la femme dont le fils est médecin')
'Lequel', 'laquelle', 'lesquels', 'lesquelles' after a preposition, with 'auquel' and 'duquel', and 'qui' after a preposition for people
'Ce qui', 'ce que', 'ce dont', 'ce à quoi' and 'tout ce que'
Demonstrative pronouns 'celui', 'celle', 'ceux', 'celles' with '-ci', '-là', 'qui', 'que', 'dont' and 'de', and the neuter 'ceci' and 'cela'
The interrogative 'lequel'

units.title: The pluperfect and telling a story
goals: Form the pluperfect with 'avoir' and 'être'
Place one past event before another
Tell a story with shifts in time
Express a regret about the past with 'si seulement'
grammar: The pluperfect: the imperfect of 'avoir' or 'être' plus the participle ('j’avais fini', 'elle était partie', 'ils s’étaient vus')
The pluperfect with the compound past and the imperfect in one story
Time shifts in a story: 'la veille', 'le lendemain', 'deux jours plus tôt', 'à ce moment-là'
'Si seulement' plus the pluperfect

units.title: The past conditional: regrets and hypotheses
goals: Form the past conditional
Express regret and reproach with 'j’aurais dû' and 'tu aurais pu'
Imagine a different past with 'si' plus the pluperfect
Report unconfirmed information with the conditional
grammar: The past conditional: the conditional of 'avoir' or 'être' plus the participle
Regret and reproach: 'j’aurais dû', 'tu aurais pu', 'il aurait fallu'
'Si' plus the pluperfect, then the past conditional, and the mixed pattern with the present conditional
The conditional for unconfirmed facts ('selon la police, le voleur serait parti')
'Manquer à' ('tu me manques'), where the subject is the one who is missed

units.title: Passive, causative and impersonal constructions
goals: Form the passive in every tense and know when French prefers 'on'
Use the pronominal passive and 'se faire' plus an infinitive
Have something done with 'faire' plus an infinitive
Use the impersonal 'il' and the indefinite words 'chacun', 'plusieurs', 'certains' and 'n’importe'
grammar: The passive: 'être' plus the participle plus 'par' or 'de', in every tense
'On' in place of a passive ('on m’a volé mon vélo')
The pronominal passive ('ça se vend bien', 'le vin blanc se boit frais')
'Faire' plus an infinitive ('je fais réparer ma voiture'), 'se faire' plus an infinitive ('il s’est fait voler son portefeuille') and 'laisser' plus an infinitive
Impersonal 'il': 'il est interdit de', 'il s’agit de', 'il reste', 'il manque'
Indefinites 'chacun', 'plusieurs', 'certains', 'n’importe qui', 'n’importe quoi', 'n’importe où'

units.title: The gerund and the present participle
goals: Form the present participle
Use 'en' plus the participle for simultaneous actions, manner and condition
Recognize the present participle in writing
Translate the English '-ing' form with the right French structure
grammar: The present participle: the stem of the present form for 'nous' plus '-ant', and 'étant', 'ayant', 'sachant'
The gerund 'en' plus the participle: at the same time, by doing, if you do; 'tout en' for contrast
The participle in writing ('les étudiants ayant fini', 'étant malade, il')
Participles versus adjectives ('fatiguant' and 'fatigant', 'différant' and 'différent')
English '-ing' in French: an infinitive, a gerund, a relative clause or 'être en train de'

units.title: Reported speech
goals: Report statements, questions and orders
Shift tenses after a reporting verb in the past
Change pronouns and time words in reported speech
Use a range of reporting verbs
grammar: Tense shifts after a past reporting verb: present to imperfect, compound past to pluperfect, future to conditional, 'aller' plus infinitive to 'allait' plus infinitive
Orders: 'de' plus an infinitive ('il m’a dit de venir')
Indirect questions with 'si', 'ce que', 'ce qui' and the question words, without inversion and without 'est-ce que'
Time and place shifts: 'aujourd’hui' to 'ce jour-là', 'demain' to 'le lendemain', 'hier' to 'la veille', 'ici' to 'là'
Everyday speech that keeps the present ('il a dit qu’il vient')

units.title: Work, administration and formal register
goals: Apply for a job and take part in an interview
Write a formal letter or email with the standard formulas
Make formal requests with the conditional and 'veuillez'
Choose between 'tu' and 'vous' at work
grammar: Letter formulas: 'Madame, Monsieur', 'Je vous écris afin de', 'Veuillez trouver ci-joint', 'Je vous prie d’agréer l’expression de mes salutations distinguées', 'Cordialement'
Formal requests: 'je souhaiterais', 'auriez-vous l’amabilité de', 'je vous serais reconnaissant de'
Inversion in formal questions
'Tu' and 'vous' in French workplaces

units.title: Opinions, news and debate
goals: Give and justify an opinion
Agree and disagree with nuance
Follow and take part in a debate on a social issue
Use the indicative and the subjunctive correctly in argument
grammar: Opinion phrases: 'à mon avis', 'd’après moi', 'je trouve que', 'il me semble que' with the indicative
Negated and questioned opinions with the subjunctive ('je ne trouve pas que ce soit juste')
Agreeing and disagreeing: 'je suis d’accord avec', 'pas tout à fait', 'tu as raison', 'avoir tort'
Argument connectors: 'd’abord', 'de plus', 'cependant', 'en effet', 'd’un côté', 'd’un autre côté'

units.title: The future perfect and the past subjunctive
goals: Form the future perfect and use it for an action completed before a future point
Use the future perfect for a supposition about the past
Form the past subjunctive and use it for an earlier action
Express degrees of probability with the indicative or the subjunctive
grammar: The future perfect: the future of 'avoir' or 'être' plus the participle, after 'quand', 'dès que', 'une fois que' and 'lorsque'
Supposition: 'il aura oublié', 'he must have forgotten'
The past subjunctive: the subjunctive of 'avoir' or 'être' plus the participle ('bien qu’il soit parti')
Degrees of probability: 'il est certain que' with the indicative; 'il se peut que' and 'il est peu probable que' with the subjunctive
The subjunctive after a superlative, 'le seul' and 'le premier' ('le meilleur film que j’aie vu')

units.title: Concession, cause and consequence
goals: Express concession and opposition with the right mood
Express cause with a range of conjunctions and prepositions
Express consequence and purpose
Build a short argued paragraph
grammar: Concession: 'bien que' and 'quoique' with the subjunctive, 'même si' with the indicative, 'malgré', 'en dépit de', 'avoir beau', 'quand bien même' with the conditional
Opposition: 'alors que', 'tandis que', 'au lieu de'
Cause: 'puisque', 'comme' at the start of a sentence, 'étant donné que', 'vu que', 'faute de', 'sous prétexte que'
Consequence and purpose: 'si bien que', 'de sorte que' with the indicative for a result and the subjunctive for a purpose, 'tellement... que', 'par conséquent', 'd’où'

units.title: Spoken French, slang and registers
goals: Understand the main features of everyday spoken French
Recognize familiar vocabulary, shortened words and the slang called 'verlan', made by reversing syllables
Move a sentence between the formal, standard and familiar registers
Know when familiar French is appropriate and when it is not
grammar: Registers: 'soutenu', 'courant', 'familier', and slang ('l’argot')
Spoken features: no 'ne', 'on' for 'nous', 'ça' for 'cela', questions without inversion ('tu vas où ?', 'c’est quoi ?')
Dislocation: 'Moi, je', 'Le café, je l’adore', 'Il est où, ton frère ?'
Shortened words ('le resto', 'la fac', 'le prof', 'l’appart') and 'verlan' ('relou', 'chelou', 'ouf')
Reduced pronunciations ('je ne sais pas' said [ʃepa]) heard in speech and not written

units.title: Emphasis and word order
goals: Highlight one part of a sentence with 'c’est... qui' and 'c’est... que'
Build emphatic sentences with 'ce qui... c’est' and 'ce que... c’est'
Recognize and use inversion after 'peut-être', 'à peine', 'aussi' and 'ainsi' in writing
Talk about art, theater and film
grammar: Cleft sentences: 'C’est Léa qui a gagné', 'C’est à Lyon que je l’ai rencontrée'
Pseudo-cleft sentences: 'Ce qui me plaît, c’est', 'Ce que je veux, c’est', 'Ce dont j’ai besoin, c’est'
Dislocation in writing and in speech, with the pronoun that resumes the moved phrase
Inversion after 'peut-être', 'à peine', 'aussi' and 'ainsi', and stylistic inversion in relative clauses ('le livre qu’a écrit mon père')
Emphatic stressed pronouns and 'même' ('moi-même', 'lui-même')

units.title: Reading literature: the past historic
goals: Recognize and understand the past historic in written narrative
Recognize the imperfect subjunctive and the past anterior in literary texts
Read a fable, a tale and a poem
Name the main figures of speech
grammar: The past historic ('le passé simple'): the '-a' type ('il parla'), the '-i' type ('il finit', 'il prit') and the '-u' type ('il fut', 'il eut', 'il put'), and 'il vint'
The past historic versus the compound past: the written narrative tense versus the spoken past
Recognition only: the imperfect subjunctive ('qu’il fût', 'qu’il eût') and the past anterior ('quand il eut fini')
Literary features: inversion after quoted speech ('dit-elle'), verse, rhyme, metaphor, simile, irony

units.title: Formal writing and argument
goals: Structure an essay in the French way: introduction, development and conclusion
Link ideas with formal connectors
Write concisely with nouns built from verbs
Apply French punctuation and spelling conventions
grammar: Essay structure: 'l’introduction' with a question to answer and a plan, 'le développement' in two or three parts, 'la conclusion'
Formal connectors: 'en outre', 'par ailleurs', 'néanmoins', 'toutefois', 'en revanche', 'en somme'
Nominalization ('augmenter' to 'l’augmentation', 'décider' to 'la décision')
Impersonal formal phrases: 'il convient de', 'il importe de', 'force est de constater'
Punctuation: spaces before ';', ':', '!' and '?', guillemets, and the traditional and reformed spellings

units.title: France: history, society and regions
goals: Read extended texts about French history and society
Narrate history with the historic present, the past historic and the passive
Read and say dates, centuries, percentages and proportions
Discuss the regions of France and the French-speaking world
grammar: The historic present in history writing, beside the compound past and the past historic
Centuries and dates in words ('au dix-huitième siècle', 'en mille sept cent quatre-vingt-neuf')
Proportions: 'vingt pour cent', 'la moitié', 'un tiers', 'la majorité de', and agreement of the verb after them
Review of the passive and of cause and consequence in history writing

units.title: B2 capstone: argument and nuance
goals: Argue a position with nuance in speech and in writing
Use every mood and tense of the course in context
Concede a point and qualify a claim
Avoid the most common B2 errors
grammar: Full review of the indicative, subjunctive, conditional, imperative and participles, and of pronoun order
Nuance: 'certes... mais', 'il n’empêche que', 'pour autant', 'du moins', 'voire'
Concessive 'quoi que', 'qui que' and 'où que' with the subjunctive
Common B2 errors: the subjunctive after 'espérer' or 'après que', 'dont', the conditional after 'si', and false friends such as 'réaliser'
